name: State Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) Services Program — Transition/Plan for Employment services for students with disabilities
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Rehabilitation Services Administration (RSA), Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services; delivered by 78 state VR agencies
amount_text: No fixed federal award to the student. RSA funds states by formula (78.7% federal share / 21.3% state share); what a student actually receives — including tuition, books, assistive technology, interpreters, tutoring — is set individually in the plan for employment/IPE by the state agency. RSA's 'Choose Work' service table lists 'Tuition Support for College Coursework' as a service available from state VR agencies (and not from Employment Networks).
eligibility: Has a physical or mental impairment that results in a substantial impediment to employment.
Requires and can benefit from VR services to achieve an employment outcome and maximize career goals.
Must be working toward, or must need VR services to reach, an employment outcome in competitive integrated employment (or supported employment).
State VR agencies must give priority to individuals with the most significant disabilities when they cannot serve everyone who is eligible.
Some states operate two agencies — one for individuals who are blind/low vision and one for all other disabilities — so apply to the right one.
Pre-employment transition services (pre-ETS) can also be provided to students with disabilities who are potentially eligible for VR, before a full eligibility determination.
The RSA program page does not state a citizenship requirement; individual state agencies set their own documentation rules — confirm with your state agency.

deadlines.label: No federal deadline — state agency semester cut-offs apply
deadlines.deadline_text: RSA does not publish a student-facing deadline. State agencies set their own; for example New York ACCES-VR requires individuals who want college training services to apply by April 15 for the fall semester and by September 15 for the spring semester.

apply_steps: Open https://rsa.ed.gov/about/states, find your state, and identify whether you need the General VR agency or the Blind VR agency.
Call or apply online with that agency's intake office and ask for an 'application for VR services' (a referral from your high school, college disability office, or American Job Center also helps).
Provide disability documentation (medical, psychological, or educational records) plus work/career goal information; the agency may do its own assessment at its expense.

If found eligible, ask the counselor to write a plan for employment / Individualized Plan for Employment (IPE) whose employment goal actually requires a college degree — services are only paid for if they appear on the signed IPE.
Complete the FAFSA first and apply for all 'comparable benefits' (Pell, state grant, veterans aid); VR pays after those, and may require you to contribute available resources.
Ask specifically for the disability-related items you need on the IPE: tuition, fees, books, assistive technology, note-taking, interpreters/CART, tutoring, and transportation.
Re-authorize funding each academic year — most agencies approve college services only one academic year at a time.
how_to_win: Name an employment goal that cannot be reached without the degree (e.g., licensed profession), because the agency must agree the degree is required for the outcome.
Show you can handle college-level work: bring recent transcripts, your high school IEP or 504 plan, evaluations, or a selective-admission acceptance letter.
File the FAFSA and state grant applications before your VR application — comparable benefits must be used first, and going in with them already done speeds up approval.
Apply before the agency's semester cut-off (New York: April 15 for fall, September 15 for spring); late files are usually pushed to the next semester.
Ask for an assistive technology evaluation at the same time — the counselor is directed to consider AT needs when assessing your ability to benefit.
Stay in contact and report grades every term; agencies can suspend college funding for failing to meet academic standards in the IPE.
documentation_required: Documentation of a physical or mental impairment creating a substantial impediment to employment; evidence you require and can benefit from VR services; academic records demonstrating ability to complete college coursework; FAFSA/financial information for the financial-need and comparable-benefits review.
notes: This is the umbrella federal program (Assistance Listing 84.126A). The student-facing interaction always happens with the state agency, and each state writes its own college-funding policy — see the New York ACCES-VR record in this file for a fully worked example with dollar caps. RSA guidance on pre-ETS was updated as recently as September 8, 2026 (rsa.ed.gov/whats-new).

name: ACCES-VR College and University Training Services (Policy 405.00) — tuition, fees, books, computer, room and board
provider: New York State Education Department, Accessibility and Vocational Rehabilitation Services — ACCES-VR
amount_text: Capped by policy for participants who meet financial need (300% of the federal poverty level threshold), after all comparable benefits: Tuition — up to the current published SUNY/CUNY or Community College rate (graduate study at private universities capped at the published SUNY graduate rate); Required academic fees — max $300 per semester, $200 per trimester, $600 per academic year; Required textbooks/materials — max $1,000 per academic year; Computer/tablet plus software — max $800, one time for the lifetime of the case; Room and board — max $1,040 per semester, $693 per trimester, $2,080 per academic year; Tutoring — max 7 hours/week at a rate not exceeding $15/hour. Full-time = 12+ credits/semester; part-time = 3-11 credits.
eligibility: Must be determined eligible for ACCES-VR services and be a 'participant' with an approved, signed IPE.
The IPE must contain an employment objective that requires a college degree, and the person must be able to complete college-level coursework.
Funding for tuition/fees/books is contingent on meeting Financial Need (threshold is 300% of the Federal Poverty Level for the household).
All comparable benefits (Pell, NYS TAP, FSEOG, veterans aid) must be applied for and used first; merit scholarships, loans and work-study are NOT counted as comparable benefits.
The college must be accredited by a U.S. Secretary of Education-recognized body or approved by the NYS Board of Regents, and be an approved ACCES-VR vendor.

Graduate school requires extra approval: a graduate degree must be required for the employment outcome or for career advancement, and the plan needs supervisor/District Office Manager/Regional Coordinator sign-off.
New York residents; students attending out-of-state schools are encouraged to also apply to that state's VR agency.

deadlines.label: Apply to ACCES-VR for fall-semester college funding
deadlines.deadline_text: "Individuals who believe that a college degree will be necessary to obtain employment in their chosen field must apply to ACCES-VR by: April 15 for the fall semester, and September 15 for the spring semester." Applicants after the cut-off may be considered starting the following semester; dates may be waived by the District Office under extenuating circumstances.

deadlines.label: Funding authorization period
deadlines.deadline_text: ACCES-VR may only authorize College Training Services up to a maximum of one academic year at a time, so renewal happens each year.

apply_steps: Apply to ACCES-VR by April 15 (fall) or September 15 (spring) — online through acces.nysed.gov or at a local ACCES-VR district office.
Supply academic evidence the counselor may request: report card, secondary school transcript, IEP or 504 plan, evaluations, or acceptance from a college with selective admissions.
Complete the FAFSA and NYS TAP and give your counselor the award information; then complete a Financial Need Review (Policy 1125.00).
Work with the counselor to write the IPE with the degree-requiring employment goal (the IPE must be written within 90 days of the eligibility determination).
Ask for each cost line separately in the IPE: tuition, required fees, books, computer/software (if required by the college or disability-related), room and board, tutoring.

Maintain academic standing — ACCES-VR can suspend college funds if you do not meet the standards and timeline in the IPE (two years for a two-year degree, four for a four-year degree, with a pro-rated extension allowance).
how_to_win: Do the FAFSA/TAP before your VR application: the policy waives the deadline only when financial aid and admission steps are already done.
Pick the most cost-effective program — the counselor is expressly told to consider cost-effectiveness, and tuition is capped at the SUNY/CUNY rate even if you attend a pricier private school.
Get documentation that a computer is required by the college or your course of study, or that it addresses a disability-related need — otherwise the $800 computer allowance will not be authorized.
Never buy non-required items with ACCES-VR funds; the policy says the agency will seek reimbursement and may re-evaluate future funding.
If you need a lighter load because of your disability, say so early: summer/mini-term funding is allowed when a disability restricts credits per semester.
For grad school, raise it no later than your junior year — it needs layered approvals and sufficient lead time before the semester starts.
documentation_required: VR eligibility documentation of disability; recent academic records (transcript, IEP/504 plan, evaluations, or standardized test scores); completed FAFSA and state aid awards; Financial Need Review showing resources; proof of acceptance/enrollment; for a computer purchase, written evidence it is required by the college or program or is disability-related.
notes: Included as a concrete, citable model of how a state 'Plan for Employment' pays college costs. Every state has an equivalent policy with different caps and dates — use the RSA state directory to find yours. ACCES-VR also publishes a Higher Education Disability Services Directory for campus offices.

name: Assistive Technology (AT) Act State Grant Program — device loan, demo, reuse and state financing through your state AT program
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Administration for Community Living (ACL), Office of Interagency Innovation / Center for Innovation and Partnership
amount_text: No student-facing federal dollar amount. ACL awards one formula grant per state, DC, Puerto Rico and each outlying territory, sized largely by state population. Services to individuals are typically free or low-cost: information/assistance and device demonstrations are usually free, device loans may carry a nominal fee to cover shipping, reutilization (reuse) devices are acquired at substantial cost savings, and state financing activities provide low-interest loans, loans guarantees or interest-rate reduction for purchasing AT.
eligibility: Any individual with a disability of any age (and their family, caregivers, or service providers) who needs an assistive technology device or service — AT Act programs are age-free, not limited to students.
You must be a resident of a state, DC, Puerto Rico or an outlying territory that receives an AT Act Section 4 grant (all 50 + DC + PR + 4 territories do).

'Assistive technology' is defined broadly: any item, device or piece of equipment used to maintain or improve independence and function — from a built-up spoon handle to eye-controlled computers — plus assessment, customization, repair and training services.
Separate Section 5 'Protection and Advocacy for AT' (PATS) grants go to each state's Protection & Advocacy agency.

deadlines.label: Rolling — no national deadline
deadlines.deadline_text: The State Grant for Assistive Technology Program is a formula grant program with no grant competitions and no published individual-applicant deadline; device loans, demonstrations and reuse inventory are requested on a rolling basis through your state program.

apply_steps: Go to the AT3 Center directory at https://at3center.net/state-at-programs/ (or https://catada.info/state.html) and select your state to get the Lead Agency, program name, phone, email and named contacts for Device Loan, Device Demo, Reutilization and Financial Loan.
Email or call the state program's information-and-assistance line first; describe the function you need (reading text, typing, hearing the TV, mobility) rather than a diagnosis.
Ask for a hands-on device demonstration, then request a short-term device loan (commonly a 30-day trial in many states) before buying anything.
If the device costs too much to buy outright, ask about the state's financing activity (low-interest loan, loan guarantee or interest-rate reduction) and about reutilization/refurbished inventory.
Ask the program to help you document the need so a VR agency, college disability office, insurer or Medicaid can co-pay.
Use the public clearinghouse https://exploreat.net/ to compare products by activity and disability before requesting equipment.
how_to_win: Named contacts are published for each activity in your state — emailing the specific Device Loan or Financial Loan contact, not a general inbox, gets a faster answer.
Borrow before you buy: a documented successful trial with a loaned device is the strongest evidence for a VR or insurer purchase request.
State AT programs will show you comparable devices at different price points — ask explicitly for a lower-cost equivalent with the same features.
Most services are free; a small loan fee covering shipping is normal, so do not assume a quoted cost means you are ineligible.
If you are a student, ask the AT program to coordinate with your campus disability office so the same device works in class and at home.
Return loans on time and report damage immediately — program goodwill and future eligibility depend on it.
documentation_required: Generally none to receive information, a demonstration or a loan; financing/loan activities require credit and income information and a purchase plan. No federal disability documentation form is specified by ACL.
notes: Program contact on the ACL page: Rob Groenendaal, Assistive Technology Program, Robert.Groenendaal@acl.hhs.gov, 202-795-7356. TA partners: AT3 Center (at3center.net, run by ATAP), CATADA (catada.info, UMass Boston), ExploreAT (exploreat.net). A separate, competitively awarded AT Alternative Financing Program (AFP) discretionary grant exists — ACL made four AFP awards in Sept 2024 and three more in Sept 2025 — but those go to organizations, not students. ABLE accounts (Reach Up To Save / Treasury) are a different program from the AT Act and are not covered here.

name: FAFSA dependency status and the 'unusual circumstances' dependency override (how students with disabilities report parent information)
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid (studentaid.gov)
amount_text: Not a fixed amount. Dependency status determines whether parent income is counted in the Student Aid Index (SAI), which drives Pell Grant and need-based aid. A dependent student who cannot provide parent information and does NOT qualify for an override is limited to a Direct Unsubsidized Loan only, with no SAI calculated.
eligibility: IMPORTANT AND COMMONLY MISSTATED: having a disability is not itself a FAFSA independent-student category. The 2027-28 dependency questions are age/date of birth (born before Jan. 1, 2004), marriage, graduate/professional enrollment, military service/veteran status, dependents you support, orphan/ward of the court/foster care since age 13, court-determined emancipation, court-determined legal guardianship, and homelessness/self-supporting-at-risk-of-homelessness.
A student who was in a court-determined legal guardianship with someone other than a parent or stepparent is independent — this is the route many students with disabilities actually qualify through.
Graduate and professional students are independent automatically.

'Unusual circumstances' that let a dependent student submit without parent information are listed by Federal Student Aid as: you or your parent are incarcerated; you left home due to an abusive or threatening environment; you have been abandoned by or estranged from your parents and have not been adopted; refugee/asylee status with parents separated or displaced; victim of human trafficking; or otherwise unable to contact or locate parents and not adopted. Disability is not on this list.
Only your college's financial aid administrator has authority to adjust dependency status; they may require documentation.
Living apart from parents, or parents not claiming you on their taxes, does NOT make you independent.

deadlines.label: Post-submission dependency review — act immediately
deadlines.deadline_text: "After submitting your FAFSA form, you must contact the financial aid office at the college or career school you plan to attend to receive information about next steps—including policies and timelines—to complete your application." No national date is published.

apply_steps: Answer the FAFSA dependency questions truthfully; if you were in a court-ordered legal guardianship or were a ward of the court/foster youth since 13, gather the court order or agency letter now.

If you are dependent but cannot safely or practically get a parent's information, select the 'unusual circumstances' path in the FAFSA form so you can skip the parent questions and submit with an interim SAI.
Contact the school's financial aid office in writing right after submitting; ask for a 'dependency override / unusual circumstances review' and ask what documentation they require.
Prepare statements from third parties (school counselor, social worker, probation or child-welfare officer, clergy, therapist) plus any court, police, or incarceration records.
If the override is denied, ask to be certified for a Direct Unsubsidized Loan as a dependent student so you at least get loan eligibility.
Note separately that students with a cognitive impairment meeting the IDEA history + CTP program test can get Pell/FSEOG/Work-Study even without a diploma (see the CTP record in this file).
how_to_win: Federal aid administrators can only override for the listed unusual circumstances — frame your file around one of them (estrangement, abuse, incarceration, trafficking) rather than around the disability itself.
Bring dated third-party documentation, not just a personal statement; the aid administrator may ask for proof of the situation.
Ask the campus disability office to co-sign or contextualize a letter about why contact with parents is unsafe or impossible — it is corroborating, not decisive.
Start the FAFSA early and treat the interim SAI as provisional; the school's final review can change your aid.
Keep the VR agency in the loop: comparable-benefit rules mean the FAFSA must be complete before VR pays tuition.
documentation_required: Court documentation of guardianship/emancipation, or documentation supporting an unusual circumstance (police/court/incarceration records, letters from a social worker, counselor, therapist or agency), plus the standard FAFSA identity, income and enrollment data.
notes: Federal Student Aid's help pages for 2026-27 and 2027-28 were checked directly. Excluded from this record: 'independent student because of disability' claims found in third-party articles — studentaid.gov does not support them.

name: Federal Pell Grant, FSEOG and Federal Work-Study for students with intellectual disabilities enrolled in a CTP program
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid (authorized by the Higher Education Opportunity Act; Comprehensive Transition and Postsecondary program designation)
amount_text: Award amounts are the standard Federal Pell Grant, Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG) and Federal Work-Study amounts set by the aid office and the annual funding formulas; studentaid.gov does not publish a separate disability-specific dollar figure. This aid is available even though the student is not required to hold a high school diploma or GED and is not required to be pursuing a degree or certificate.
eligibility: Has a cognitive impairment characterized by significant limitations in intellectual and cognitive functioning and adaptive behavior as expressed in conceptual, social and practical adaptive skills.
Is currently, or was formerly, eligible for special education and related services under IDEA — including if determined eligible under IDEA while homeschooled or attending private school.

Is enrolled or accepted for enrollment in a comprehensive transition and postsecondary (CTP) program for students with intellectual disabilities at a college or career/trade school that participates in federal student aid.
Is maintaining satisfactory academic progress.
Meets the basic federal student aid requirements except the high school diploma/GED and degree/certificate-seeking requirements.

The CTP program must be one approved by the U.S. Department of Education; the published list of approved schools (as of July 9, 2025) is on the studentaid.gov page and covers dozens of institutions in most states.

CTP programs must have the student participate, for at least half the program, in credit-bearing enrollment, auditing/participating with nondisabled students, noncredit courses with nondisabled students, or internships/work-based training with nondisabled individuals.

deadlines.label: Program-specific; no single federal date
deadlines.deadline_text: studentaid.gov publishes no deadline. CTP programs set their own application deadlines and are listed school-by-school; "If you have questions about your eligibility, contact the financial aid office at your college or career school."

apply_steps: Open the studentaid.gov CTP page and find the approved CTP programs in your state (the list is organized by state, e.g. Auburn University, Jacksonville State University, University of South Alabama in Alabama).
Confirm the program is a designated CTP program that participates in federal student aid — ask the program director in writing.
Gather IDEA documentation proving you are or were eligible for special education and related services, plus current evaluation evidence of intellectual and adaptive-functioning limitations.
Apply to the CTP program and get an acceptance/enrollment letter.
File the FAFSA; tell the school's financial aid office you are applying as a CTP student with an intellectual disability so they apply the exception to the diploma/degree-seeking rules.
Ask the aid office about the CTP program's own charges (some charge a separate program fee in addition to or instead of standard tuition) and how Pell/FSEOG/Work-Study can be applied to it.
how_to_win: Do not let a school's financial aid system auto-reject you for lacking a diploma/GED — cite the CTP exception on the studentaid.gov eligibility page and ask for a manual review.
IDEA eligibility from years ago counts ('currently, or were formerly, eligible'), so dig out old IEPs and eligibility paperwork rather than paying for a new assessment.
Pick a program where you will be included with nondisabled students for at least half the activity — the CTP designation requires it, and undocumented inclusion can sink the aid.
Federal Work-Study at a CTP school is a realistic way to add earnings without affecting SSI the way unreported wages can — talk to a WIPA benefits planner first.
Apply to more than one approved CTP program in your state; seats are limited even though the federal aid is not.
documentation_required: Evidence of IDEA special-education eligibility (current or former) and of the qualifying cognitive/adaptive impairment; acceptance or enrollment in a Department of Education-approved CTP program; standard FAFSA identity and residency documentation.
notes: This is the real 'Pell for students with IDD' provision. It is program-gated: the student must be in a federally approved CTP program, not merely identify as having an intellectual disability. Think College's directory (separate record) lists inclusive programs, but only the studentaid.gov list is CTP-approved for federal aid.

name: Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) Discharge of federal student loans and TEACH Grant service obligations
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid
amount_text: 100% discharge of the borrower's federal student loan debt: William D. Ford Federal Direct Loans, Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) Program loans, and Federal Perkins Loans. A TPD discharge also relieves the borrower of a TEACH Grant service obligation. Payments received after the qualifying effective date are refunded.
eligibility: The borrower must be total and permanently disabled as defined by the program.

Qualification routes published on the page: (1) qualifying U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) documentation, (2) qualifying Social Security Administration (SSA) documentation, or (3) certification by an authorized medical professional (their email address, or their signature on the completed application).
Some borrowers qualify automatically and others must apply.
A three-year monitoring period applies to discharges based on SSA or medical certifications; loan obligations may be reinstated if conditions are not met during that period.
Eligible-loan questions: 888-303-7818.

deadlines.label: No application deadline
deadlines.deadline_text: Federal Student Aid publishes no deadline for a TPD discharge application; it can be filed any time. Borrowers can separately initiate a 120-day payment pause while applying.

apply_steps: Decide which route you will use — VA determination, SSA determination, or an authorized medical professional's certification — because the documents differ.
Gather the documentation for that route (VA decision letter, SSA award/notice letter, or the certifying clinician's name, email and signature).
Apply online through the TPD discharge application on studentaid.gov and upload your documents; manual submission by mail, fax or the upload tool is also offered.
If you want immediate relief, submit the application or contact Federal Student Aid to have payments paused for 120 days while you apply.
If your loan holder asks you to keep paying during review, call your servicer.
Calendar the three-year monitoring period conditions if your discharge is SSA- or physician-based.
how_to_win: Use the SSA route if you already have a fully disabling SSA determination — it needs no new medical paperwork and can qualify you automatically.
A VA rating documentation route avoids the physician certification step entirely.
Give the medical professional their own email address ready to hand to the system; electronic certification is the fastest path and the review will stall without it.
Ask about the 120-day payment pause on day one rather than waiting for delinquency.
Note that discharged amounts may have tax consequences and can affect future Title IV aid eligibility — get that explained before you sign.
documentation_required: One of: qualifying VA documentation; qualifying SSA documentation; or an authorized medical professional's electronic certification/signature on the completed TPD application, plus the standard discharge application.
notes: Relevant to graduate students and to students whose disability prevents completion. Distinct from the (real but separate) closed-school, fraud-to-vest and borrowed-teacher discharges; no 'TEACH grant forgiveness for disability-related teaching' provision is claimed here beyond the service-obligation relief stated on the page.

name: Social Security work incentives for students who work: SEIE, subsidy/special conditions (Reduction of SGA), 1619(a)/(b) — plus free WIPA benefits counseling
provider: U.S. Social Security Administration (Office of Employment Support Initiatives) — Red Book / Ticket to Work
amount_text: 2026 figures published by SSA: Student Earned Income Exclusion (SEIE, SSI only) — $2,410 of earnings excluded per month up to $9,730 per year for SSI recipients under 22 who are regularly attending school. SGA (2026): $1,690/month for disabilities other than blindness; $2,830/month for statutorily blind beneficiaries. Trial Work Period (TWP) monthly threshold (2026): $1,210. SSI Federal Benefit Rate (2026): $994 individual / $1,491 couple. Continued Medicare Part A premium option at 45% reduction: $311/month (base $565). These are not grants — they let a student earn work income and pay for work supports without losing cash benefits or Medicaid/Medicare.
eligibility: SEIE: SSI recipient under age 22 who is regularly attending school and receiving earned income. 'Regularly attending school' at college level means taking one or more courses and attending classes at least 8 hours a week (12 hours/week for grades 7-12; 12, or 15 with shop practice, for a training course preparing for employment), or less for reasons beyond the student's control such as illness.
SEIE applies automatically in qualifying months and is counted before the general and earned income exclusions.

Subsidy and Special Conditions (sometimes called Reduction of SGA): applies when an employer or a support system (job coach, extra supervision, reduced or easier duties, extra breaks as an accommodation, help supplied by a VR agency) means your pay exceeds the real value of the work — SSA then uses only the real value of your work when deciding SGA. Available under both SSDI and SSI for SGA decisions (not used when computing the monthly SSI payment amount).
Impairment-Related Work Expenses (IRWE): the cost of certain items and services you pay out of pocket and need in order to work is deducted from gross earnings in the SGA decision.

Unsuccessful Work Attempt (UWA): work started or intensified but stopped or reduced below SGA within six months because of the disability (or loss of extra help) is not counted in the SGA decision; a UWA cannot occur during the Trial Work Period.

Medicaid While Working (1619(b)) and 1619(a): cash benefits can stop while Medicaid coverage continues when earnings rise; SSA publishes yearly state threshold amounts (2026 thresholds available through the Red Book).
Ticket to Work participation is free and voluntary and unlocks state VR agencies, Employment Networks, and Work Incentives Planning & Assistance (WIPA) projects at no cost.
Wage reporting: since April 2025 SSA can pull monthly wage data from participating payroll providers with your permission (form SSA-8240).

deadlines.label: Ongoing duty — report work activity
deadlines.deadline_text: There is no application deadline for work incentives; SSA requires that you report work activity and earnings, and states that beneficiaries should consult a certified benefits counselor before entering the workforce and whenever an increase in earnings is expected. Work Incentive Seminar Events (WISE) are held on the fourth Wednesday of each month at 3:00 p.m. ET.

apply_steps: Call the Beneficiary Call Center at 866-968-7842 (or 866-833-2967 TDD) with general work-incentive questions.

Find your regional WIPA project through the 'Find Help' map on Choose Work and book a free session with a Community Work Incentives Coordinator (CWIC) before you accept a job, internship, co-op or paid work-study position.
Register with Ticket to Work (or with your state VR agency as your Employment Network-equivalent) to get free employment services and a work/incentives plan.
Confirm you meet the SEIE school-attendance test: for college, keep enrollment at or above 8 contact hours per week and save your schedule or enrollment verification.
Track and keep receipts for impairment-related work expenses (attendant care, equipment, modified vehicle, therapy copays) and tell your CWIC to apply them to the SGA calculation.
Ask your VR agency to document any job coach or on-the-job support in writing — that documentation is what establishes 'subsidy or special conditions' for Reduction of SGA.
If you want SSA to receive wages automatically, complete and submit form SSA-8240 to authorize the Payroll Information Exchange.
how_to_win: Talk to a CWIC before every raise, extra semester of work-study, or graduation into full-time work — most benefit losses come from unreported or misunderstood income changes, not from the rules.
Use the SEIE deliberately: it excludes $2,410/month up to $9,730/year, so concentrating campus employment in the school-year months maximizes it before the annual cap is reached.
Under 22 and in college is exactly the SEIE target population — do not assume an internship salary will reduce your SSI check; report the hours and it often will not.
Keep a written record of extra supervision or reduced duties from your employer; SSA uses only the real value of work performed when subsidy or special conditions exist.
Remember that 1619(b) can keep Medicaid even when the SSI check stops — that is the coverage that often pays for campus and post-graduation services.
Read the Red Book ('A Guide to Work Incentives', SSA Publication No. 64-030, June 2026 edition) and the 'What's New in 2026' page before relying on older dollar figures from any website.
documentation_required: Proof of SSI/SSDI receipt; enrollment verification and class schedule showing at least 8 hours/week of college attendance for SEIE; pay stubs/employer statements; receipts for impairment-related work expenses; employer or VR-agency statements documenting job coaching, extra supervision or reduced duties for subsidy/special-conditions findings.
notes: Excluded after verification: the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC). The IRS page (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/work-opportunity-tax-credit) states the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 extended WOTC only until December 31, 2025 and that it is available for wages paid to individuals who begin work on or before December 31, 2025 — so it is not claimable for 2026 hires and should not be listed as student funding. 'SSWIM' could not be verified as a live program and is excluded. Ticket to Work service-provider comparison table confirms that tuition support for college coursework comes from state VR agencies, not Employment Networks.

name: National Federation of the Blind Scholarship Program
provider: National Federation of the Blind (NFB)
amount_text: NFB awards more than $300,000 in cash and prizes each year across all 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico; NFB states there are "thirty $10,000 merit-based scholarships currently available." Individual awards are not need-based; finalists receive financial assistance to attend the national convention.
eligibility: Must be legally blind in both eyes, with a Confirmation of Legal Blindness form submitted.
Must reside in the United States, the District of Columbia, or Puerto Rico.
Must be 18 years of age by July 3 of the application year (the 2026 cycle used July 3, 2026).
Must be pursuing or planning to pursue a full-time post-secondary course of study in a degree program at a United States institution in the fall of the application year.
Part-time students: NFB may award up to five scholarships annually to applicants enrolled part-time who meet all other requirements (recognizing employment, caregiving, or ongoing medical care).
Must participate in person in the entire NFB National Convention and in all scheduled scholarship program activities.
Graduate and undergraduate students in degree programs are both covered.

deadlines.label: Applications open
deadlines.deadline_text: "Applications Open: December 1" — NFB states 'The 2027 scholarship application will open in December.'

deadlines.label: Deadline to submit complete application
deadlines.deadline_text: "Deadline to Submit Complete Application: March 31." The applicant must press submit, and must contact their NFB state affiliate president by phone or email to request an interview by March 31 (interviews may occur in early April without affecting eligibility).

apply_steps: Start the online application at https://scholarships.nfb.org/ after December 1; you can save and return to it.
Have your eye-care professional complete the Confirmation of Legal Blindness form and upload it.
Read the 2026 Scholarship Submissions Checklist and FAQs on the application site before writing anything.
Prepare the required essay (the checklist describes one essay, limited to 700 words or less) and at least one letter of recommendation.
Contact your NFB state affiliate president directly to request your interview — email nfb.org/about-us/state-affiliates contacts by March 31.
Confirm your submission: you must receive an email confirmation and must have pressed 'submit'; otherwise the application is not considered.
Plan and budget to attend the full NFB National Convention in person in July if you are named a finalist (financial assistance to attend is provided to finalists).
how_to_win: NFB awards on academic excellence, community service and leadership — write the 700-word essay around demonstrated leadership in blindness issues, not around medical history.
The interview is mandatory and is scheduled by your state affiliate president: the single most common failure mode is not reaching out to that person before March 31.
Get the legal-blindness certification form signed weeks early; an application missing it is incomplete regardless of merit.
If you attend part-time, use the application's dedicated part-time section to explain employment, caregiving or medical treatment — that is the route to one of the five part-time awards.
Log in after submitting and verify the confirmation email actually arrived; NFB explicitly warns that no confirmation means no submission.
Email scholarships@nfb.org or call 410-659-9314 ext. 2415 (Cayte Mendez, Scholarship Committee Chair) with eligibility questions rather than guessing.
documentation_required: Confirmation of Legal Blindness (form, from an eye care professional); completed application form; one essay of 700 words or fewer; at least one letter of recommendation; transcript/enrollment evidence for a U.S. degree program; completed interview with an NFB state affiliate.
notes: NFB also runs state-level affiliate scholarships with separate (often earlier) deadlines — e.g., several affiliates report February or June state deadlines — verify with your affiliate. Largest scholarship program of its kind in the U.S. per NFB.

name: AFB Scholars Program (Lulu J. Alonso Scholarship Fund) — Science & Technology, Research, and Aging & Vision Loss pathways
provider: American Foundation for the Blind (AFB)
amount_text: Three tiers, renewable annually: Community College $8,000; Undergraduate $20,000; Graduate $28,000.
eligibility: Blind students (legally blind; verification required) enrolled or accepted in a full-time postsecondary program.
Legal blindness is defined as an individual who cannot see better than 20/200 with correction or whose visual field in the best eye is 20 degrees or less at the widest diameter with correction.
Age: must be 18 years or older by the start of the upcoming Fall semester.
Academic enrollment: enrolled or planning to enroll as a full-time student in a degree-seeking program at an accredited institution for the upcoming Fall semester.
Minimum cumulative 3.0 GPA.
Science & Technology Scholarship: undergraduate students studying STEM fields such as computer science, engineering, biology, mathematics or information technology.
Research Scholarship: graduate students (undergraduates considered) conducting research during the academic year under the supervision of a university advisor.
Aging & Vision Loss Scholarship: students pursuing a degree in Gerontology, or a degree in Public Health, Vision Rehabilitation, Social Work or Psychology together with a certificate in Gerontology.

Scholar obligations: participate in mentorship activities with AFB Leaders, participate in one approved annual conference with staff, and submit an end-of-year narrative reflecting on academic and professional growth.

apply_steps: Watch afb.org/get-involved/afb-scholars-program from early January; the application window is short (about six weeks).
Choose one pathway — Science & Technology (undergraduate STEM), Research (grad research with an advisor), or Aging & Vision Loss (gerontology degree or related degree plus a gerontology certificate).
Collect verification of legal blindness and an official transcript showing a cumulative 3.0 GPA or higher.
For the Research pathway, get your faculty advisor to describe the supervised research you will conduct during the academic year.
Email inclusivefuture@afb.org with questions before the deadline.
Plan to attend one approved annual conference with AFB staff and to complete the mentorship and year-end narrative requirements if selected.
how_to_win: The award is explicitly about creating blind leaders: AFB's stated goal is to 'cultivate future blind leaders,' so show advocacy, mentorship participation and a change-agent narrative, not just grades.
Match your pathway precisely — a STEM undergrad who applies to the Research pathway will not be competitive; the requirements differ by pathway.
The 3.0 GPA floor and full-time enrollment are hard gates; fix an official transcript before the application, not after.
Because awards are renewable annually, treat the end-of-year narrative as an application for year two and submit it on time.
AFB also co-funds scholarships with the American Council of the Blind — apply to both programs in the same cycle (see the ACB record).
Download and circulate the program flier through your school's services-for-blind-students office; it lists the eligibility summary and often surfaces deadlines earlier than social media.
documentation_required: Official documentation verifying legal blindness status — AFB lists medical records, vocational rehabilitation documentation (on letterhead), NLS registration, etc.; official transcript evidencing cumulative 3.0 GPA; proof of full-time degree-seeking enrollment or acceptance at an accredited institution; for the Research pathway, evidence of supervised research; conference, mentorship and year-end narrative commitments once awarded.

name: ACB Scholarship Program (American Council of the Blind, in partnership with AFB and other sponsors)
provider: American Council of the Blind (ACB)
amount_text: Scholarships ranging from $2,000 to $7,500 for entering freshmen, undergraduates, graduate students, and students attending technical college. In 2026 ACB awarded $112,300 in scholarships to 21 students.
eligibility: Must be legally blind, defined on the page as not able to see better than 20/200 in the best eye with glasses or contact lenses, or a visual field in the best eye of 20 degrees or less at the widest diameter with correction.
Must maintain a 3.0 GPA to be eligible for most scholarships in the program (unless extenuating circumstances exist).
Must be a full-time student, or a part-time student who works at least 32 hours per week.
Must be involved in their school and local community.
Must attend a post-secondary institution in the United States.
Entering freshmen, current undergraduates, transfer students and graduate students are all eligible (document type differs by category — see documentation).

apply_steps: Register for an ACB online account first — you cannot reach the scholarship application without one; then log in and open the application from the link at the top of the site.
Obtain a certification of legal blindness from an ophthalmologist, optometrist or physician.
Upload the right transcript: high school transcript for entering freshmen; current-school transcript for continuing students; undergraduate transcript for graduate applicants.
Secure two letters of recommendation from a current or recent instructor, career counselor or employer, and submit each letter separately.
Upload proof of acceptance from a post-secondary school (a notice or letter from the admissions office); students continuing at the same school they attended in 2025/2026 do not need this.
Submit during the November 1 - February 14 window and be prepared to attend ACB's National Conference and Convention in July as a recipient.
how_to_win: The program has many named sub-scholarships funded by partners — one complete application is reviewed against them, so submit early and completely rather than cherry-picking.
Two recommendation letters must come from instructors, career counselors or employers and must be submitted separately; late letters are a common disqualifier.
The part-time route exists only if you work at least 32 hours per week — include proof of hours if you are not full-time.
Assistive technology costs are an eligible use of the award ('other additional costs associated with assistive technology'), so write your request around concrete AT and tuition needs.
Winners are expected to attend the ACB convention; say yes in the application and arrange transportation/support early.
Create the ACB account in November, not in February — the account step plus separate letter uploads take real time.
documentation_required: Certification of legal blindness from an ophthalmologist, optometrist or physician; transcript (high school, current, or undergraduate as applicable); two letters of recommendation submitted separately; proof of acceptance/enrollment from a U.S. post-secondary institution.
notes: ACB's program has run since 1982 and is administered jointly with AFB-supported funds; AFB's own page confirms AFB 'provides financial support each year to students who are blind in partnership with the American Council of the Blind.' Apply to NFB and AFB programs too — they are separate.

name: Gallaudet University Merit-Based and Endowed Scholarships for deaf and hard of hearing students
provider: Gallaudet University — Office of Financial Aid (Washington, DC)
amount_text: 'These scholarships range in dollar value and are awarded for up to four years of study for first-time freshmen, and three years of study for transfer students.' No dollar figure is published on the page.
eligibility: Merit-Based Scholarships: open to all undergraduate deaf and hard of hearing students whose academic achievements are exemplary; awarded to incoming deaf/HoH freshmen and new transfer students by the Admissions Office.
All newly admitted students are automatically considered for merit scholarships — no separate application.

Endowed Scholarships: awarded by the Financial Aid Office by matching students to donor-established criteria; most are restricted to U.S. citizens or U.S. permanent residents holding an I-151, I-551 or I-551C (Permanent Resident Card).
Many endowed scholarships have a financial-need criterion, so the FAFSA and the general university scholarship application are strongly suggested.
Contact: financial.aid@gallaudet.edu, (202) 651-5290 / (202) 618-6844.

deadlines.label: Tied to admission and FAFSA, not to a separate scholarship date
deadlines.deadline_text: The scholarship page publishes no standalone deadline. Consideration for merit awards is automatic for newly admitted students; need-based endowed awards depend on submitting the FAFSA and the general university scholarship application.

apply_steps: Apply for admission to Gallaudet as a deaf or hard of hearing applicant; merit scholarship consideration is automatic on admission.
Submit the FAFSA listing Gallaudet's school code so need-based endowed awards can be calculated.
Complete Gallaudet's general university scholarship application through the Financial Aid Office.
If you are a permanent resident, have your I-151/I-551/I-551C ready — most endowed awards require it.
Email or call financial.aid@gallaudet.edu / (202) 651-5290 to ask which endowed scholarships match your major and circumstances.
Also pursue the outside scholarships Gallaudet's page points to (its 'Potential Outside Scholarship Sources' list) and stack them with institutional aid.
how_to_win: There is no separate merit application — academic record at admission is the whole contest, so strengthen the application file itself.
Transfer students get up to three years of merit funding; submit the transfer transcript early because the merit pool is admissions-driven.
File the FAFSA even if you think you do not need it — most endowed awards have a need criterion and the office cannot match you without the data.
Ask the Financial Aid Office for the current list of endowed awards restricted to your program (education, STEM, humanities, accessibility-related fields recur often).
Use Gallaudet's own contact lines; the office explicitly handles matching students to donor criteria.
documentation_required: Admission application and academic transcripts; FAFSA; general university scholarship application; U.S. citizenship or permanent resident card (I-151/I-551/I-551C) for most endowed awards; documentation of hearing status for deaf/HoH-restricted awards.
notes: Gallaudet is the federally chartered university for deaf and hard of hearing students; institutional aid is listed here because most deaf/HoH-specific national scholarships are affiliate- or state-level. The Alexander Graham Bell Association's 2026 aid listing (https://agbell.org/financial-aid/) shows its postschool programs for 2026 are limited — its college-age offering listed for 2026 is the George H. Nofer Scholarship for Law (up to three graduate law students at $5,000; the 2026 window closed March 9, 2026), and all AG Bell awards require documentation of bilateral hearing loss in the moderately-severe to profound range plus use of listening and spoken language.

name: INCIGHT Scholarship for students with disabilities
provider: INCIGHT (501(c)(3), Portland, Oregon)
amount_text: "Typically the INCIGHT Scholarship award amount is $500 and increases for scholars that reapply." Funds are disbursed half in the Fall and half in the Winter and are sent directly to the school, never to students.
eligibility: Must be a current resident of Washington, Oregon or California — explicitly NOT open to students nationwide.

Must have a disability as defined by the ADA, DSM-V, IDEA or other governing body; the published list includes autism, deaf-blindness, deafness, developmental delay, emotional disturbance, hearing impairment, intellectual disability, multiple disabilities, orthopedic impairment, other health impairment, specific learning disability, speech or language impairment, traumatic brain injury, and visual impairment including blindness.
Must be attending higher education during the funding cycle following the application (college, university, community college, graduate program, or vocational/technical school, any degree type).
Must be enrolled at your school and able to provide enrollment verification.
Open to graduating high school seniors and adult students.
Financial need is NOT considered; grades are considered but are not a deciding factor.
Recipients must complete either 30 hours of community service or volunteer at one INCIGHT event.

deadlines.deadline_text: "The application deadline for the 2026 - 2027 school year is April 15, 2026. All application materials must be received by midnight on the date in order for the application to be reviewed." The site states the 2026-2027 application is closed. Recipients are notified in June.

apply_steps: Confirm you are a resident of Oregon, Washington or California.
In the spring, open https://www.incight.org/scholarship and complete the online application (the application is only available online).
Have disability documentation ready: ADA/DSM-V/IDEA classification, Social Security award showing an ADA-covered disability, or an IEP/504 plan for high school students.
Obtain enrollment verification from your college, university, community college, graduate program or vocational school.
Write about community involvement and obstacles overcome — those, not financial need, are the stated basis for selection.
Confirm every field is complete and that the application actually submitted (the applicant bears this responsibility).
Email scholarship@incight.org with eligibility or troubleshooting questions.
If awarded, plan the 30-hour community service commitment or one INCIGHT event volunteer shift.
how_to_win: Lead with documented community involvement; the program's stated purpose is to recognize students who show outstanding service to their community and motivation to attend higher education.
Do not lead with financial hardship — need is expressly not a factor.
Any ADA/DSM-V/IDEA-defined disability qualifies, including conditions students often exclude themselves over (emotional disturbance, other health impairment, TBI, developmental delay). Apply anyway.
Re-apply every year: the award amount increases for returning scholars, and you may apply as long as you remain in school.
Submit enrollment verification before the deadline rather than after; it is an explicit requirement.
Because funds go to the school, coordinate with your financial aid office in advance about how a $500+ award will be applied so it does not displace need-based aid.
documentation_required: Documentation of a disability per ADA / DSM-V / IDEA (an IEP or 504 plan qualifies high school applicants; Social Security benefits covered by ADA qualify); enrollment verification from the postsecondary institution.
notes: Third-party sites list an April 15, 2027 deadline; the official page only states the 2026-2027 (April 15, 2026) cycle, so the 2027 date is not asserted here.

name: AAHD Frederick J. Krause Scholarship on Health and Disability
provider: American Association on Health and Disability (AAHD)
amount_text: "Scholarships are generally for $1,000 but amounts are at the discretion of the AAHD Board of Directors Scholarship Committee and based on availability of funds." The Committee also decides how many scholarships are awarded each year.
eligibility: Undergraduates: must be enrolled full-time and have completed at least one full year of college — sophomore status or greater as of the coming fall. High school students entering college for the first time are NOT eligible (exception: high school students who earned sophomore status via AP credits).
Graduate students: may be enrolled part-time or full-time in a graduate school pursuing a post-graduate degree.
Applicants must have a disability as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act and must provide documentation verifying it.

Preference for students majoring in public health, health promotion, disability studies, disability research, rehabilitation engineering, audiology, disability policy, special education, or other fields related to disability and health.
Preference for students with a history of community service and/or volunteer activities.
Must be a U.S. citizen or legal resident living in the United States and enrolled in an accredited United States university.
Previous AAHD winners may not re-apply unless they enroll in a new program of study (e.g., moving from undergraduate to a master's, or master's to PhD).
Those who serve on the Disability and Health Journal Editorial Board are not eligible.

apply_steps: Wait for the window to open by November 2026 for the 2027 cycle and watch https://aahd.us/initiatives/scholarship/.

Write a Personal Statement (maximum 2 pages, double spaced) covering brief personal history, educational/career goals, extra-curricular activities, community service, and why you should be selected. It must be written solely by the applicant.
Request one letter of recommendation from a faculty member or academic advisor; it must carry the writer's signature and your name must be clear on the document.
Obtain an official or unofficial copy of your most recent college transcript.
Assemble disability documentation from a specialist (physician, educator, etc.) verifying your disability status.
Compile everything into a single submission through the SurveyMonkey application portal AAHD links on the page.
Accept the clause allowing AAHD to use your name, photo and/or story in future scholarship materials.
Email scholarship@aahd.us if you need accommodations to the application process or have questions.
how_to_win: This is a health-and-disability scholarship: name a major or career direction in the preferred list (public health, disability studies, health promotion, rehabilitation engineering, audiology, disability policy, special education, disability research) and connect your own disability to it.
Community service history is an explicit preference — quantify hours and outcomes in the personal statement.
AAHD states the statement must be written solely by the applicant; do not use AI or ghostwriters, and do not exceed 2 double-spaced pages.
You need a faculty/advisor letter, not a personal reference; ask early in the fall term.
First-generation college freshmen are ineligible — apply after you have completed a year, or as a graduate student where part-time enrollment is allowed.
Ask for application accommodations proactively; the page invites contact for accommodations to the application process.
documentation_required: Disability documentation from a specialist (physician, educator, et al.) verifying ADA-defined disability status; most recent college transcript (official or unofficial); one signed faculty/advisor letter of recommendation; 2-page double-spaced personal statement.

The Epilepsy Foundation's own scholarship list points to this AAHD program plus the UCB Family Epilepsy Scholarship, NYU Langone medical scholarships, GW's disability scholarship page and Patient Advocate Foundation (https://www.epilepsy.com/parents-and-caregivers/work-college/scholarships).

name: Anne Ford Scholarship (and the Allegra Ford Thomas Scholarship) for graduating high school seniors with a documented learning disability
provider: National Center for Learning Disabilities (NCLD)
amount_text: Anne Ford Scholarship: $10,000 total, paid $2,500/year over four years. Allegra Ford Thomas Scholarship (sibling award from the same NCLD program): $5,000 total, paid $2,500 each year over two years.
eligibility: Anne Ford: a graduating high school senior who will enroll in a full-time bachelor's degree program in the fall.

Allegra Ford Thomas: a graduating high school senior who will enroll in a two-year community college, a vocational or technical training program, or a specialized program for students with disabilities in the fall.
Applicants must have a documented learning disability (LD).
Students who have Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) together with a learning disability are encouraged to apply — ADHD alone is not the qualifying basis as stated.
Selection is by NCLD; the application page also points to its NCLD help-line (301-966-2234).

deadlines.deadline_text: "Applications are now open and will be reviewed on a rolling basis until Sunday, May 10, 2026." Apply early because review is rolling.

deadlines.label: Stated application period on NCLD's open-scholarships page
deadlines.deadline_text: "Application Period: November 1 to April 17 ... Selection Process: Rolling basis ... The application period will close on April 17." (NCLD's announcement page for the two scholarships; the individual award pages show the rolling review end-date, so check both in the spring.)

apply_steps: Confirm you have a documented learning disability; gather the evaluation that establishes it (a formal diagnosis is required at the time of application).
Open https://ncld.org/scholarships-awards/anne-ford-scholarship/ in the winter and start the online application.

Choose the right award: Anne Ford if you are entering a four-year bachelor's program full-time; Allegra Ford Thomas if you are entering a two-year college, vocational/technical program, or a specialized program for students with disabilities.
Write the required essay/personal statement about your educational journey, the challenges you have faced and your aspirations.
Arrange recommendation letters and have your school issue an official transcript.
Submit well before the April 17 - May 10 window closes since applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.
how_to_win: Rolling review means the earliest complete files have the advantage — submit in the first weeks of the window, not the last day.
Documentation of the LD is a gate, not a formality: an IEP or 504 plan plus the underlying psychoeducational evaluation is the strongest package.
If you have both an LD and ADHD, say so explicitly — NCLD encourages those applicants and the combination is common among winners.
NCLD's stated framing is resilience and determination; write about specific barriers and the strategies that work for you rather than generic goals.
Apply to both NCLD awards if your post-secondary plan is uncertain between a four-year and a two-year/vocational route, and to the Learning Disabilities Association and Lime Connect awards as well.
Ask your school counselor to send the transcript directly and early; incomplete files stall rolling review.
documentation_required: Proof of a documented learning disability (formal diagnosis / psychoeducational evaluation; IEP or 504 plan records); academic transcripts; personal statement/essay; letters of recommendation.
notes: NCLD's page describing the application period (Nov 1 - April 17) was written for the 2024 cycle and is still live, while the Anne Ford award page states a May 10, 2026 rolling-review end. Both dates are reported here because the official pages are inconsistent; confirm the current window before applying.

name: PAF Scholarships for Survivors (cancer and chronic illness)
provider: Patient Advocate Foundation (PAF)
amount_text: No per-award amount is published on the page. PAF states that over 20 years it (with donors) has provided 235 scholarships totaling over $1 million, and that 40 students are currently funded.
eligibility: Must be a Citizen of the United States (the program purpose text also refers to legal U.S. residents).
Must be under the age of 25.
Must have been diagnosed with and/or actively treated for cancer or a chronic disease within the past five years.

Diagnosis counts as active/eligible if you are currently and actively being treated and managed, and/or have been actively treated in the past five years — examples given include current chemotherapy, radiation or anti-neoplastic drug therapy; current drug therapy for a chronic illness; current pathology revealing cancer/chronic illness; newly diagnosed and awaiting treatment; affirmation of current disease management; or the cancerous organ removed with ongoing treatment.
Open to students pursuing undergraduate or graduate studies.
Requires demonstrated academic achievement, community service, and financial need.

deadlines.label: 2026-2027 academic term deadline (closed)
deadlines.deadline_text: "Deadline for submissions was March 5, 2026, and applications for the 2026–2027 academic term are now closed."

apply_steps: Ask your treating physician, oncologist, primary care physician or nurse to complete the Diagnosis Verification Form, or to write a signed letter on practice letterhead containing: patient name, diagnosis, date of diagnosis, when active treatment began/will begin, and when it ended/will end (chronic illnesses do not require an end date).
Complete the Scholarship for Survivors application in full.
Write the required essay (500-word minimum, 2,000-word maximum) on how your diagnosis has impacted your life and future goals.
Upload a copy of your college/university acceptance letter, or list the schools you applied to if you have not been accepted yet (acceptance is verified for winners).

Upload two letters of recommendation from non-related people (teachers, coaches, community leaders) that endorse your character, academics and work/volunteer experience and include the writer's name, address and phone number.
Provide a copy of your official transcript (an official transcript is required before funds are distributed).

Complete the financial form showing need, and include a copy of the first two pages of the tax return of whoever claims you as a dependent; if $0 income or no return was filed, complete the Declaration of Income Form.
Submit early in the cycle (the deadline is in early March) and plan on notification roughly 3-4 months later.
how_to_win: The two letters are described by PAF as 'an important part of your application' — choose recommenders who can speak to both academics and character, and make sure they include their address and phone number in the letter.
Keep your diagnosis verification current and inside the five-year active-treatment window; an old diagnosis without ongoing treatment or management will not qualify.
Stay within 500-2,000 words on the essay — over-length submissions are a technical failure.
Because funds are distributed to your college and an official transcript is required, contact your financial aid office early about how the award will interact with your existing aid.
The under-25 age cap closes the door permanently — apply in your earliest eligible year and re-apply each cycle if not selected.
PAF also runs separate case-management services; enrolling in those does not substitute for the scholarship application but its staff can help you document the medical-necessity story.
documentation_required: Diagnosis Verification Form (or provider letter on letterhead with name, diagnosis, diagnosis date, treatment start/end); completed application; 500-2,000 word essay; acceptance letter or list of schools applied to; two non-relative recommendation letters with writer contact details; official transcript copy; financial form plus first two pages of the dependent-claimant's tax return or a Declaration of Income Form.
notes: Chronic-illness category. Award is open to undergraduates and graduates but the published eligibility bullets on the page are for the National Undergraduate award; graduate applicants should request the graduate guidelines from PAF before filing.

provider: Lime Connect, in partnership with Johnson & Johnson

Must be a current undergraduate, graduate, MBA or PhD student attending a 4-year university in the United States.
Must be enrolled at the university either Spring, Summer or Fall of 2027.
Must be pursuing a Health Care or STEM-based degree with a desire to pursue a career in Health Care.
Must be actively engaged in driving disability inclusion.
Lime Connect describes its network as high-achieving students and professionals (including veterans) with visible and non-visible disabilities.

Log in to the Lime Community Platform, then open 'Jobs and Programs' and select the Johnson & Johnson Access-Ability Lime Scholarship apply button.
Enter contact and education information and upload a current resume/CV.
Upload a copy of your current university transcripts.
Answer the three essay questions about your career goals in the healthcare industry and about driving disability inclusion.
Request one letter of reference from a professor, advisor or supervisor, and make sure it is submitted by the separate recommendation deadline one week after yours.
Confirm you will be enrolled in Spring, Summer or Fall 2027 at a 4-year U.S. university in a Health Care or STEM program.

One reference letter is required, but it is due a week later than your application: brief your recommender with your resume and a sentence about why you are applying so it is not late.

name: The Quell Foundation Fighter Scholarship (students in treatment for a diagnosed mental health condition)
provider: The Quell Foundation
amount_text: Award amount is not stated on the official scholarships page.
eligibility: High school seniors, or current undergraduate or graduate students, who are being treated for a diagnosed mental health condition.
Minimum GPA of 3.20 for the Fighter Scholarship (the Foundation's Survivor and First Responder Legacy awards require 3.50).
Requires documentation from a mental health professional that you are active in services.
Requires two letters of recommendation (professor, coach, counselor or manager).
Requires an academic transcript, a personal statement, and a Form 1040, Student Aid Report, or Tax Return Form.
