apply_steps: Monitor https://thequellfoundation.org/scholarships/ for the next opening and subscribe to the Foundation's newsletter if offered.
Ask your treating mental health professional for a current letter confirming you are active in services — this is the eligibility core of the award.
Request two recommenders from professors, a coach, counselor or manager.
Assemble your academic transcript showing a 3.20+ GPA.
Write the personal statement.
Prepare your financial document: Form 1040, Student Aid Report, or Tax Return Form.
Submit the full package when the portal opens; the same materials also qualify you to consider the Foundation's other awards if you fit them.
how_to_win: The distinguishing document is proof of active treatment, not a diagnosis alone — get the clinician letter dated close to the submission window.
The 3.20 GPA floor is lower than the Foundation's other awards; do not confuse it with the 3.50 requirement for the Survivor and First Responder Legacy scholarships.
Include the exact financial document listed (1040, SAR or tax return form) — missing tax paperwork is the likeliest completeness failure.

Because the Foundation's stated purpose is improving care and treatment for people with mental health challenges, write about recovery, treatment engagement and reduced stigma rather than minimizing the condition.
Also consider the Foundation's Bridge the Gap Clinical Licensure Grant if you already hold a master's in a mental health field — it is rolling, not annual.
documentation_required: Documentation from a mental health professional that the applicant is active in services; academic transcript; personal statement; two letters of recommendation (professor, coach, counselor or manager); Form 1040, Student Aid Report, or Tax Return Form.
notes: Psychiatric-disability coverage. Third-party listings describe it as a 'Fighter Scholarship' for students living with a diagnosed mental health condition; the official page is the controlling description. Applications were closed on 2026-09-15.

name: Maryland Assistive Technology Loan Program (ATLP) — low-interest financing for AT equipment
provider: Maryland Department of Disabilities / Maryland Technology Assistance Program (MDTAP), a state Assistive Technology Act program
amount_text: Borrow from $500 to $70,000: unsecured AT loans up to $10,000; unsecured vehicle and home-modification loans up to $20,000; non-adapted vehicles up to $40,000; adapted vehicles up to $70,000 (restrictions apply). All loans are below-market and fixed for the loan term; rates depend on creditworthiness and are disclosed at application processing and approval.
eligibility: Maryland resident with a disability (the borrower may be the person with a disability, a family member, a friend, or anyone intending to buy AT for a Maryland resident with a disability).
The loan must be used to purchase assistive technology that helps the resident live, work and learn more independently.

Eligible equipment includes home modifications, adapted and non-adapted vehicles, scooters and wheelchairs, Braille equipment, hearing and vision aids, augmentative communication devices, environmental control units, and computers with adaptive peripherals.

Approval is not automatic: the program reviews income-to-debt ratio, stability of residence and job, payment history with existing creditors, and financial ability to repay. Criteria are explicitly less stringent than a bank's.
Two approval paths: approved by the lender at a discounted interest rate, or approved by the ATLP at a discounted interest rate.

deadlines.label: Rolling
deadlines.deadline_text: No deadline is published; applications are accepted on a rolling basis and interest rates are subject to change.

apply_steps: Confirm the item you want counts as assistive technology under the program's list (equipment that helps a Maryland resident with a disability live, work and learn more independently).
Complete and submit the ATLP application online, or download the ATLP application and email it with supporting documents to MDTAP (the address is on the program page).
Include purchase information for the equipment and the vendor.
Provide income, residence and credit information so the program can assess income-to-debt, stability and payment history.
Choose the approval path offered to you — lender-approved with a discounted rate, or ATLP-approved with a discounted rate — and confirm the fixed rate at approval.
Ask MDTAP's other AT services at the same time (device reutilization, device loan and demonstration) so you do not finance equipment you could borrow or obtain refurbished.
how_to_win: Anyone may be the borrower if the equipment is for a Maryland resident with a disability — a parent or friend with better credit can apply.
Pair the loan with a short-term device loan or demonstration from the same state program so you prove the device works before financing it.
Check the reutilization/refurbished inventory first; the AT Act reuse route can cut the financed amount dramatically.
The program's underwriting is deliberately looser than a bank's — a prior bank decline is not a reason to skip the application.
For vehicles, note the different caps ($40,000 non-adapted vs $70,000 adapted) and that restrictions apply, so get the adaptation specification in writing from the vendor.
Because rates vary with creditworthiness and are only disclosed at processing, apply well before you need the equipment.
documentation_required: ATLP application with supporting documents; proof the purchase is assistive technology for a Maryland resident with a disability; financial information (income, existing debt, residence and job stability, creditor payment history); vendor/purchase details.
notes: A worked example of the AT Act 'state financing activity' allowed under the federal program. Equivalent programs in other states are listed at https://www.ntac.blind.msstate.edu/resources/assistive-technology-low-interest-financing-programs (National Technical Assistance Center, Mississippi State University) and in the AT3 Center state directory.

name: Electronic Equipment Tech Loan — Texas School for the Blind and Visually Impaired (TSBVI) Outreach
provider: Texas School for the Blind and Visually Impaired (TSBVI), Outreach Programs (Texas Education Agency)
amount_text: No money is paid to students — equipment is lent at no purchase cost for a three-month loan period, extendable at the end of three months if another district has not requested the item. Electronic Equipment inventory includes CCTV video magnifiers, handheld video magnifiers, refreshable Braille displays and Braille notetakers; a separate Active Learning Tech Loan inventory includes Essef Boards, HOPSA Dresses, Little Rooms and Resonance/Vibration Boards. The program was established through the Hoblitzelle Foundation plus federal funds awarded through the Texas Education Agency.
eligibility: A statewide Texas resource: equipment is available for loan to any student in Texas who is eligible for services as a student with a visual impairment.
Requests are made through a receiving agency/district (the school district or program that will hold the equipment), not by an individual student or family directly.
A local agency must sign the loan agreement accepting responsibility for use, repair and return of the equipment.
The item must be available in the TSBVI Outreach inventory — availability is confirmed with the AT consultant before the application link is issued.
Related categories: Electronic Equipment (3-month loans) and Active Learning equipment and materials.

deadlines.label: Rolling, with a 3-month loan term
deadlines.deadline_text: No application deadline; loans run for three months and "Loans may be extended at the end of three months if another district has not requested the item(s) your student is using."

apply_steps: Contact Carrie Gillespie, Assistive Technology Consultant at TSBVI Outreach, to discuss the student's needs, determine the best device, and confirm it is available.
You will then receive a link to the Electronic Equipment Tech Loan Application; complete it.
TSBVI prepares a written agreement detailing the items and the receiving agency's responsibilities for use, repair and return.
The loan agreement is sent via DocuSign; a local agency (school district or program) must sign accepting responsibility.
Equipment ships to the receiving agency; if the device is damaged or lost, contact TSBVI Outreach to coordinate repair.
At the end of the loan, the borrowing agency returns the equipment via UPS, USPS or FedEx to: TSBVI Warehouse, Attn: Carrie Gillespie, 1100 W. 45th Street, Austin, Texas 78756.
Do NOT ship returned items as 'Free Matter for the Blind' — the borrowing agency is financially responsible for replacing equipment lost that way.
how_to_win: Call/email the named AT consultant before applying — the application link is issued only after availability is confirmed, so a vague request wastes a cycle.
Route the request through your school district's VI teacher or service-agency staff, because a local agency must sign the DocuSense agreement.
Ask about the Active Learning Tech Loan at the same time if the need is orientation/mobility or concept-development materials rather than electronics.
Tell the consultant the assessment or trial purpose ('evaluate whether this refreshable braille display works for coursework') so they recommend comparable devices.
Request an extension before the three-month mark, and check whether another district has the item queued.
Pair the loan with a request for APH (American Printing House) materials through the same TSBVI Outreach services page.
documentation_required: Completed Electronic Equipment Tech Loan Application; a signed agency loan agreement (via DocuSign) accepting responsibility for use, repair and return; eligibility of the student for services as a student with a visual impairment in Texas.
notes: Included as a concrete, currently-published 'how to request equipment' pathway with a named contact. Note the loan is made to an agency on the student's behalf, which is typical of state device-loan programs. TSBVI Outreach also coordinates APH (American Printing House) materials.

name: Think College Search Tool — national directory of Inclusive Postsecondary Education (IPSE) programs for students with intellectual disability
provider: Think College (Community Living and Participatory Action Research / Think Highered), funded by the U.S. Department of Education
amount_text: Not a funding award. The directory itself lists 324 inclusive postsecondary education (IPSE) programs and 51 other programs for students with intellectual disability connected with colleges and universities.
eligibility: Students with intellectual disability seeking college attendance at an accredited institution of higher education.
An IPSE Program is defined as a program where students with intellectual disability can take typical college classes at an accredited institution — for credit, audit, or continuing education.
All listed programs must be affiliated with an accredited college or university and must serve students with intellectual disabilities.

Some listed programs only serve students who are still receiving services from their high school; those can be filtered out with the 'Remove Programs that ONLY Serve Students in High School' checkbox.
Age ranges vary by program (e.g., the TAPESTRY entry at University of Alaska Anchorage serves ages 18-26).

deadlines.label: Directory has no deadline; each program sets its own
deadlines.deadline_text: Think College publishes no directory-level deadline. Application dates, age limits and fees are set program-by-program and appear on each listing; most programs admit for the fall term.

apply_steps: Search https://thinkcollege.net/college-search by state and filter out high-school-only programs if you are age-out eligible.
Use the 'save/favorites' feature to build a comparison list — the tool lets you save, compare and download basic information for each program.
Work through Think College's 'Conducting a College Search: Questions to Ask College Programs', which features over 60 questions to ask programs.
Read the 2026 student-facing publication 'A Student's Guide to Finding the Right College' before visiting campuses.
Contact the named program coordinator and email listed on each entry to ask about application deadlines, cost, ages served, financial aid eligibility (CTP designation) and campus housing.
For each shortlisted program, confirm on the studentaid.gov CTP list whether the program is approved for federal Pell/FSEOG/Work-Study (see the CTP record in this file).
how_to_win: Programs list a named contact person — emailing that coordinator directly, not the general admissions office, is what actually gets an application packet.
Ask whether the program is federally designated as a CTP program; that single fact determines whether a student can hold Pell, FSEOG and Work-Study.
Use the 60+ question checklist to compare programs on credit-bearing enrollment with nondisabled peers, employment/internships, and independent living supports.
Note the disclaimer: listings are self-submitted and do not imply Think College endorsement, so verify every claim with the campus directly.
Many programs require that the student still be in an IDEA eligibility window — check the age-out rule (commonly 21-26) before investing in an application.
If you know of a program that is not listed, Think College accepts new listings by email, so ask a campus program to add itself.
documentation_required: None for the directory. Individual IPSE programs typically require IDEA eligibility documentation, a psychoeducational evaluation showing intellectual disability, transition paperwork, and an application fee set by the institution.
notes: This is the only national directory of college programs for students with intellectual disability. Think College also publishes an annual 'Program Update' count of IPSE programs.

name: AHEAD — Association on Higher Education And Disability (professional association and searchable directory of campus disability resource professionals)
provider: AHEAD (Association on Higher Education And Disability), founded 1977
amount_text: Not a student funding award. AHEAD is a membership association; its published professional membership level is $325 (Full Professional Membership). It reports approximately 3,700 members across all 50 states and 10+ countries, plus formal partnerships with 37 regional affiliates.
eligibility: Membership-based directory — AHEAD describes itself as the leading professional membership association for individuals committed to equity for persons with disabilities in higher education, and maintains a searchable membership directory.
Members include disability resource professionals, student affairs personnel, ADA coordinators, diversity officers, AT/IT staff, faculty and instructional personnel.
Open to individuals, institutions and organizations; AHEAD's own site describes the join/renew process and membership levels.

Students CAN join: AHEAD's Student Membership is for individuals whose primary involvement with higher education is as a currently enrolled undergraduate or graduate student who is interested in engaging with work that enhances postsecondary access for persons with disabilities (individuals employed full-time by a higher education institution are not eligible for Student Membership; Student Members may not hold office on the Board but may vote for AHEAD offices).
There is no student eligibility test — students interact with AHEAD members (campus disability services staff) rather than with AHEAD as an aid program.

deadlines.label: None — association membership and directory are continuously available
deadlines.deadline_text: AHEAD publishes no directory deadline. Annual conference registration opens each year (the site announced 'REGISTRATION NOW OPEN' for AHEAD events and for its online instructor-led courses on an ongoing basis).

apply_steps: Use AHEAD to identify and reach the disability resource office leadership at a specific campus, or to find your regional AHEAD affiliate.
Students and families: search the campus's own disability services office first (AHEAD members run those offices), then contact AHEAD's office if you need help escalating an access problem.
Professionals/staff: join or renew at https://www.ahead.org/join/levels to access the searchable membership directory and the Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability (JPED).
Ask your campus disability services coordinator whether they are an AHEAD member — it is a useful signal about the office's professional grounding when you are choosing a college.
Attend or register for AHEAD's annual conference and online instructor-led courses for documentation-standards and accommodation guidance.
how_to_win: When comparing colleges, use AHEAD membership (and its 37 regional affiliates) as a proxy for whether a campus has a professionally staffed disability office rather than an ad hoc arrangement.
AHEAD's publications and webinars describe current documentation practice — read them before you assemble accommodation paperwork, since standards vary by institution.
If a campus office is unresponsive, an AHEAD regional affiliate contact can point you to comparable institutions.

Keep in mind the directory is member-facing: for a public list of campus offices, pair AHEAD with your state VR agency's higher-education disability services directory (e.g., New York's ACCES-VR lists one).
documentation_required: Not applicable for students (no student application). Membership requires an institutional or professional affiliation for full professional membership.
notes: Included as a professional-association directory of the people who run campus accommodation, AT and accessibility policy. AHEAD's site reports membership of ~3,700; some pages state 'over 5,000' / 'over 6,500' — figures differ across pages, so the about-page number is used here.

name: ADA National Network — 10 regional ADA Centers providing free technical assistance on postsecondary accommodation rights
provider: ADA National Network, funded by NIDILRR (Administration for Community Living), coordinated through the National Council on Independent Living
amount_text: Free information, guidance and training — no cash benefits. Call 1-800-949-4232 (voice/relay) and find your regional center at adata.org.
eligibility: Anyone may call or email: individuals with disabilities, businesses, employers, state and local governments, architects, disability organizations, school personnel.
The Network serves questions under the ADA plus related laws it can route (Fair Housing Act, IDEA, Rehabilitation Act/Section 504).

Postsecondary coverage: Title II of the ADA covers publicly funded universities, community colleges and vocational schools; Title III covers privately funded schools; all schools receiving federal funding must comply with Section 504.
All programs of a postsecondary institution, including extracurricular activities, must be accessible.

deadlines.label: None — open intake by phone/email
deadlines.deadline_text: No deadline; assistance is available on request through 1-800 calls, email and in-person consultations with an ADA specialist in your region.

apply_steps: Call 1-800-949-4232 (V/TTY) or use adata.org to find your regional ADA Center.
Before the call, write down the institution, the accommodation requested, the date you requested it, and the school's written response.
Ask the specialist to confirm whether your school is covered by Title II, Title III, and/or Section 504, and what the school's obligation actually is.

Request the Center's postsecondary materials — the 'Postsecondary Institutions and Students with Disabilities' fact sheet and the research briefs 'Higher Education and the ADA' and 'Digital Access for Students in Higher Education and the ADA'.
If the campus denies or delays an accommodation, ask the specialist how to file with the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights.
Ask for training if your campus is unfamiliar with a specific need (interpreters/CART, accessible digital materials, service animals in housing).
how_to_win: Cite the standard the specialist gives you in writing to the campus office — schools respond faster to a request that references Section 504/Title II correctly.

Remember the two lawful refusals: no accommodation is required if it fundamentally alters the program or creates an undue financial/administrative burden. Frame your request so neither applies (e.g., extended test time does not change the substantive content).
Do not wait for orientation — the ADA FAQ advises notifying the campus office 'well in advance' of the needed modification.
Ask about effective communication specifically (interpreters, CART, Braille/electronic formats, assistive listening) — these are program-access duties, not discretionary favors.
For housing, invoke both the ADA/504 duty of comparable, convenient, accessible housing at the same cost and, where relevant, the Fair Housing Act.
Regional centers are subject-matter experts on your state's institutions — use the same center repeatedly rather than calling a national hotline.
documentation_required: None to receive technical assistance. To press an accommodation request you will want your own disability documentation and a written record of requests and responses.
notes: The ADA National Network is the closest thing to a 'campus disability center' resource at the federal level: 10 regional ADA Centers plus the ADA Knowledge Translation Center (ADAKTC) and ADA-PARC. Excluded from this file: the HEATH Resource Center — https://www.heath.gwu.edu and https://heath.gwu.edu returned no live page (404/proxy error) when checked on 2026-09-15, so no working official URL could be verified.

name: What colleges legally must (and need not) provide: Section 504 / ADA Title II academic adjustments — ED Office for Civil Rights guidance
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
amount_text: No money changes hands. Academic adjustments must be provided at no charge to the qualified student; the school may not charge a student with a disability more than others for the program, and must give surcharges only where it charges all students for that service.
eligibility: You must be a qualified student with a disability — that is, have a disability AND meet the essential prerequisites and standards for admission or participation.
A school may not deny admission because you have a disability if you meet the essential requirements for admission.

Disclosure is voluntary, but if you want an academic adjustment you must identify yourself as having a disability; the school is not required to identify you or assess your needs (unlike a school district's FAPE duty).
Postsecondary schools are NOT required to provide FAPE; they must provide appropriate academic adjustments to avoid discrimination.
If the school provides housing to nondisabled students, it must provide comparable, convenient and accessible housing to students with disabilities at the same cost.

deadlines.label: No statutory deadline — request early; delivery is not immediate
deadlines.deadline_text: OCR states that a postsecondary school does not have to provide the adjustment you requested on the day you ask, but it must provide it in time if it is to be effective — "if the school determines that it is appropriate to provide an academic adjustment, it must provide it in a timely manner." Practice on campus is to request at registration and re-request every semester.

apply_steps: Before enrolling, contact the campus disability/accommodations office and ask for its written documentation requirements and its intake procedure.
Self-identify in writing and submit current documentation (diagnosis, date, how reached, credentials of the professional, functional impact on a major life activity, and academic impact).

Request specific adjustments tied to the barrier (priority registration, reduced course load, course substitutions, note takers, recording devices, sign language interpreters, extended testing time, a TTY in your dorm room, screen-reading/voice-recognition software on school computers).
Participate in the school's review; remember the school may offer an effective alternative or conduct its own evaluation at its own expense.
Re-activate your accommodations each semester, and meet each instructor to arrange implementation.
If the response is inadequate, use the school's internal grievance procedure and file a complaint with OCR (the school must have at least one employee designated to coordinate 504 compliance).
how_to_win: Under the ADA Amendments Act the interpretation of 'disability' is broader than in older OCR guidance, but 'qualified' still controls — show you meet the essential prerequisites and standards of the program.
Bring documentation that maps the functional limitation to a specific academic task; an IEP or 504 plan alone is often not enough, though it can help identify supports that worked.
Ask for adjustments that do not alter essential requirements: extended time is required; changing the substantive content of an exam is not.

Do not ask for personal items - schools are expressly not required to provide personal attendants, individually prescribed devices, readers for personal use or study, or other devices or services of a personal nature such as tutoring and typing; finance your own device through VR or your state AT program and ask the school to permit its use in class.
If an interpreter or CART is needed, request it at registration — auxiliary aids must be furnished in a timely manner, and if you are still being evaluated the school must provide interim aids.
Keep everything in writing, and calendar the follow-up: the school is not required to second-guess a student who never re-requests.
documentation_required: Current documentation showing the presence of a diagnosed disability and its current impact — commonly: diagnosis and supporting information (date of diagnosis, how it was reached, credentials of the diagnosing professional), how the disability affects a major life activity, and how it affects academic performance. Schools may set reasonable standards and may require a report prepared by an appropriate professional; IEP/504 plans are helpful but may be insufficient on their own.
notes: This is the Section 504 / ADA obligations summary requested. Companion OCR documents verified: 'Auxiliary Aids and Services for Postsecondary Students with Disabilities' (https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/individuals-disabilities/auxiliary-aids-and-services-for-postsecondary-students-with-disabilities) and the OCR topic page 'Disability Discrimination: Academic Adjustments for Postsecondary Students' (https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/disability-discrimination/disability-discrimination-key-issues/disability-discrimination-academic-adjustments-postsecondary-students, last reviewed January 14, 2025) with its 'Individualized Assessments for Students with Disabilities in Postsecondary Education' guidance PDF.

name: How a campus accommodation intake actually works — UC Berkeley Disabled Students' Program (DSP) five-step first-time process
provider: Disabled Students' Program (DSP), UC Berkeley — Division of Equity & Inclusion (student-facing DSS office)
amount_text: Accommodation coordination services are provided by the university; DSP does not publish an award amount. DSP runs auxiliary service units (e.g., Alternative Media) whose services are requested each semester.
eligibility: Open to admitted degree students, Summer Sessions students, and students studying abroad at UC Berkeley, including graduate students.

Students applying for accommodations for the first time must complete all five steps: (1) apply online; (2) provide DSP with documentation of your disability; (3) contact DSP to schedule a one-hour intake appointment; (4) attend the intake appointment; (5) request your accommodation letters and services each semester.
Disability documentation must verify two things: (1) the presence of a diagnosed disability or medical condition, and (2) the current impact of that condition.
Students are responsible for initiating the request and providing medical documentation; DSP does not identify students or assess needs proactively.
Applying creates a DSP account that keeps medical documentation and disability information separate from other University records.

deadlines.label: Documentation must precede the intake appointment
deadlines.deadline_text: "Documentation must be submitted to DSP in advance of scheduling your intake appointment." Students must complete all five steps before they may be approved for DSP services.

deadlines.label: Per-semester: letters and services
deadlines.deadline_text: "Request your accommodation letters and services every semester as soon as you have registered for classes." Alternative media services must be requested each semester via AIM.

apply_steps: Complete DSP's online application (this creates your DSP account).
Have your provider send documentation to you first so you can review it, then upload it with the application; alternatively email dsp@berkeley.edu or fax (510) 643-9686.
Use DSP's documentation requirements page and the provider forms it publishes to give your clinician.
Email dsp@berkeley.edu to schedule the one-hour intake appointment with a Disability Specialist.
Attend the intake and discuss the impact of your disability, your academic program, and the accommodations/services you may need for equal access.
Log into AIM after registering for classes and request accommodation letters for each course.
Meet each instructor to confirm the accommodation will be implemented on time; use your specialist's Calendly link (or dsp@berkeley.edu) for follow-up changes.
how_to_win: Documentation is the bottleneck and must address CURRENT impact, not just diagnosis — ask your clinician to describe functional limitations in academic settings.
Submit documentation before you email for an appointment; DSP will not schedule the intake without it.
Request accommodation letters the day registration closes; interpreter, note-taking, CART and alternative media all need lead time.
Book the follow-up appointment with your Disability Specialist early in the term if your needs change — modifications after intake are handled through the specialist, not through a new application.
Letters do not disclose your diagnosis to faculty; expect an accommodation statement without the condition named (DSP's own FAQ explains why).
If you need alternative media (Braille, e-text, enlarged print), log into AIM and request it each semester — it does not carry over automatically.
documentation_required: Documentation verifying (a) a diagnosed disability or medical condition and (b) its current impact; DSP supplies forms clinicians can complete; the requirement is described per disability type on DSP's 'Documentation for DSP' page.
notes: Chosen as a fully documented, current public example of a major research university's DSS intake; the five-step sequence (apply → document → intake → approve → per-semester letters) is close to standard practice. UC Berkeley graduate students can also call DSP at (510) 642-0518.

name: Campus accommodation documentation and semester timing — Cornell University Student Disability Services (SDS)
provider: Student Disability Services (SDS), Cornell University
amount_text: No charges to students for approved academic accommodations or aids/services coordinated by SDS.
eligibility: Students with documented disabilities may be eligible for academic accommodations; approvals rest on disability documentation, academic history, and the student's own account of their needs.
Registration begins with completing the online Disability Self-Disclosure Form (self-identification is voluntary but required to receive accommodations).
You may meet with SDS before supplying documentation and SDS will guide you on what is needed.

Accommodation plans are individually tailored; typical approvals include exam modifications (extended time, reduced-distraction location, computer use), assistive technology, removal of physical barriers, and print material in alternative formats (Braille, e-text, enlarged print).
Additional aids (test-taking computer use, sign language interpreting, note-taking, accessible course materials) require completion of SDS-specific forms and advance notice.
The Law School's accommodation process differs from the rest of the university.

deadlines.label: Accommodation letters each semester
deadlines.deadline_text: "You will need to request an Accommodation Letters within the first two weeks of classes, or at least two weeks before accommodations are expected to begin (if accommodations were granted or modified once the semester has started)." (No calendar date is published; the rule is the first two weeks of each term.)

deadlines.label: Advance notice for other aids and services
deadlines.deadline_text: Interpreting, note-taking, accessible course materials and test-taking computers "require advance notice to SDS in order to be available when you need them." No fixed number of days is published.

apply_steps: Complete the online Disability Self-Disclosure Form (from https://sds.cornell.edu/forms).

Assemble any helpful documentation: educational records such as a high school IEP or 504 plan, a neuropsychological or educational evaluation, a statement from a health/mental health provider (using SDS's published statement guidelines), medical records, audiology report, vision assessment, vocational assessment, or proof of accommodations used on standardized exams (SAT/ACT).

Where SDS has a matching form, have your provider complete the Mental Health Disability Assessment Form, the Medical Documentation of Asthma and Allergy Disabilities Form, or the Medical Documentation of a Physical or Chronic Medical Disability Form.
Submit documents in an accepted format: PDF, Microsoft Office (DOC/DOCX), text, JPG/JPEG or PNG. No HEIC files and no password-protected files unless you give the password.
Meet with SDS to develop your academic accommodation plan.
Each semester, request accommodation letters for each course within the first two weeks and meet with instructors to arrange implementation; repeat if you change section/lecture.
For an emotional support animal or other housing-related need, follow SDS's separate ESA guidelines (Cornell reviews ESA approval annually).
how_to_win: SDS explicitly says it does not 'medicalize' the process and will work with students who cannot obtain documentation — file anyway and explain the barrier on the form rather than delaying.
There is no SDS form for ADHD or learning disabilities; instead submit the psychoeducational evaluation, IEP/504 plan or standardized-test accommodation history that SDS lists as helpful.
The two-week letter window is a real cut-off — request letters on the day you finish registration, and ask about 'timely notice' with the instructor if a course starts differently.
Interpreters, note-takers and accessible materials need advance notice: send those forms the same week you send your letters.

Send unencrypted, openable files (PDF/DOCX/PNG/JPG) - a rejected HEIC or password-protected file silently delays your review; keep your plan current, since accommodations require your involvement every semester and ESA re-approval is annual.
Law students: use the Law School's handbook process instead of the general SDS route.
documentation_required: Disability Self-Disclosure Form plus documentation of the disabling condition and its functional impact. Acceptable evidence includes IEP/504 plans, neuropsychological or educational evaluations, provider statements (SDS supplies provider statement guidelines), medical records, audiology reports, vision assessments, vocational assessments, and proof of prior testing accommodations. SDS also provides disability-specific assessment forms for mental health, asthma/allergy, and physical or chronic medical disabilities.
notes: Chosen because it publishes both the acceptable documentation set and the concrete per-semester timing rule, and because it states plainly what happens when documentation is unavailable — an important practical contrast to Berkeley. Related Cornell pages: https://sds.cornell.edu/ , https://sds.cornell.edu/forms , https://sds.cornell.edu/get-started/confidentiality , https://sds.cornell.edu/esa-guidelines
